notes.meaning: Jacob learned that grain was available in Egypt and challenged his sons for just looking at one another. They were frozen with indecision and fear while the famine worsened around them. Jacob urged them to take action rather than sitting in helpless despair.

Jacob told his sons to travel down to Egypt right away to buy grain so the family would survive. God had made food available, so Jacob expected his household to use ordinary means rather than waiting for a miracle. Providing for a family requires practical effort and care.
Ten of Joseph's brothers set out together on the long journey to Egypt. They travelled as a large group for safety on the road and to bring back enough grain for their large households.

Jacob refused to let Benjamin go with his brothers because he feared some harm might come to him. Benjamin was the only remaining son of his beloved wife Rachel living at home, and Jacob could not bear the thought of losing him too.
The sons of Jacob arrived in Egypt alongside many other travelers seeking food. The famine had spread across Canaan as well, forcing people from all over the region to look to Egypt for help.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern critical scholars view the repeated mention of the famine as evidence that different written sources were joined together.

notes.meaning: Joseph had full authority over the land of Egypt and oversaw the sale of grain to foreign buyers. When the brothers came into his presence, they bowed low with their faces to the ground. Without knowing it, they were beginning to fulfill the dreams Joseph had shared with them many years earlier.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Catholic teaching noted that Joseph wisely sold the grain rather than handing it out freely, ensuring that the supply would last for everyone.

notes.meaning: Joseph recognized his brothers immediately, but he hid who he was and spoke to them in a stern, rough tone. He asked where they had come from, and they answered that they were from Canaan to buy food. Joseph acted like a stranger to test them and see if their character had changed.

Joseph knew his brothers, but they did not recognize him at all. More than twenty years had passed, and he was now a grown man dressed in Egyptian royal robes and speaking a foreign tongue. They never imagined that the brother they sold into slavery was now the ruler of Egypt.

Seeing them bow reminded Joseph of the prophetic dreams God gave him as a boy. He accused them of being spies who had come to inspect the land's weak and undefended borders. He pressed this charge to draw out information about his father and Benjamin.
The brothers denied the accusation with deep respect, calling Joseph their lord. They insisted that they were his humble servants who had come only to buy food during the famine.

They defended themselves by explaining that they were all sons of one man. No father would risk ten of his own sons at once on a dangerous mission like spying. This family bond was their proof that they were honest men.

Joseph refused to accept their defense and insisted they had come to search out the land's vulnerabilities. He kept up the pressure so they would feel the need to explain their family history in even greater detail.

The brothers explained that they had originally been twelve brothers from the land of Canaan. They reported that their youngest brother was back home with their father and that one brother was no more. They assumed Joseph was dead, unaware they were speaking to him directly.
Joseph repeated his charge that they were spies to keep testing their story. He treated their shifting explanations as a reason to doubt their honesty until they could prove what they said.

Joseph laid down a test, swearing by Pharaoh's life that they would not leave until their youngest brother came to Egypt. He proposed holding nine of them in prison while one went home to fetch Benjamin. This demand was designed to discover whether Benjamin was alive and how they treated him.

Joseph locked all ten brothers in prison together for three days. This brief taste of confinement forced them to stop and reflect on the pain they had once caused Joseph when they threw him into a pit.
On the third day, Joseph returned and told them, 'I fear God. Do this and you will live.' By saying he feared God, he reassured them that he would act justly and not abuse his power.

Joseph softened his original plan by offering to hold just one brother hostage while the other nine carried grain home to their starving families. They would only have to return with their youngest brother to prove their honesty and save their lives. They agreed to these terms, grateful that their households would not starve.

Under this sudden pressure, the brothers began confessing their guilt to one another. They remembered Joseph's terror and how he had begged them for mercy, but they had refused to listen. They recognized that their current trouble was God bringing their past cruelty back upon them.
Reuben reminded his brothers that he had pleaded with them not to harm the boy, but they had ignored his warnings. He told them they were now facing a reckoning for Joseph's blood.
The brothers did not know that Joseph understood everything they were saying among themselves. He had been using an Egyptian interpreter to disguise the fact that he spoke their native Hebrew.

Overwhelmed with emotion at their remorse, Joseph had to turn away from them to weep. When he regained his composure, he took Simeon and had him bound in front of them as the hostage. Simeon was likely chosen as the next oldest after Reuben or as a leader in their past wrongdoing.

Joseph secretly ordered his servants to fill their sacks with grain, place each man's silver back into his bag, and give them provisions for the journey. He loved his family and could not bring himself to take money from them for their bread.

The brothers loaded the heavy sacks of grain onto their donkeys and started on their way home. They left Egypt with the food they needed, but with heavy hearts because Simeon remained behind in chains.
When they stopped for the night at a roadside camp, one brother opened his sack to feed his donkey and found his silver lying right at the top. The sudden sight of the returned money startled him.

He told his brothers that his money was back in his sack, and their hearts sank with sudden dread. Instead of celebrating a free gift, their guilty consciences made them tremble and ask what God was doing to them. They feared they were being framed for theft.
When the brothers reached Canaan, they gave their father Jacob a complete account of their journey. They needed to explain why they had returned without Simeon and what had happened in Egypt.
They reported that the ruler of Egypt had spoken harshly to them and treated them as enemy spies. They described how frightening and demanding the governor had been.

They recounted how they had defended their family honor, telling the ruler they were honest men and not spies. They had explained their history as twelve brothers, mentioning that one was gone and the youngest was still home with their father.

The brothers explained the ruler's condition: he kept one brother and allowed them to bring food home, but insisted they bring Benjamin back with them. Only by presenting Benjamin could they prove their honesty, free Simeon, and be permitted to trade in the land.

As each brother emptied out his sack, every man discovered his own bundle of silver inside. Seeing all the money returned filled both the brothers and Jacob with panic, fearing they would be treated as thieves on their next visit.

Jacob broke out in grief, accusing his sons of robbing him of his children. He believed Joseph was dead, Simeon was lost, and now Benjamin was about to be taken away. In his deep sorrow, Jacob felt that everything was working against his good.

Reuben tried to ease his father's fears by offering the lives of his two sons if he failed to bring Benjamin safely back. Though Reuben meant this as a solemn promise to protect Benjamin, it was a reckless and impossible pledge for a father to make.

Jacob gave a flat refusal, declaring that Benjamin would not go down to Egypt. He explained that Benjamin was the only son of Rachel left with him, and warned that any harm coming to the lad would send his gray head down to the grave in unbearable grief.
